extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, USPTO examiners, IP litigators, and IP law students
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for assessing inventive step/non-obviousness under United States patent law (35 U.S.C. §103), including USPTO/MPEP rationales, PHOSITA, Graham factors, TSM, hindsight avoidance, and use of secondary considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. § 103 — non-obvious subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may not be obtained if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the statutory standard by comparing claimed subject matter as a whole to prior art from the perspective of PHOSITA. Consider entire specification when determining obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP rationales for concluding obviousness (A) Combining prior art elements
rubrics_metrics.description: "Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results" is a rationale that may support a finding of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If known elements are combined using known methods and result is predictable to PHOSITA, the combination may be obvious. Consider whether combination merely yields expected results.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP rationales for concluding obviousness (B) Simple substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: "Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results" is a recognized rationale for obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether substituting one known element for another would have been within the routine skill of PHOSITA yielding predictable outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP rationales for concluding obviousness (C) Use of known technique to improve similar devices
rubrics_metrics.description: "Use of known technique to improve similar devices (methods, or products) in the same way" can support obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether a known technique, applied to a similar device, would predictably improve it in the asserted manner to PHOSITA.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP rationales for concluding obviousness (D) Applying a known technique to a known device
rubrics_metrics.description: "Applying a known technique to a known device [...] ready for improvement to yield predictable results" is a rationale for obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the device was 'ready for improvement' and whether applying the known technique would produce predictable results to PHOSITA.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP rationales for concluding obviousness (E) Obvious to try
rubrics_metrics.description: "Obvious to try – choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, with a reasonable expectation of success" may indicate obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where there is a design need or market pressure and a finite, predictable set of options, pursuing known options that lead to anticipated success can be "ordinary" and support obviousness. Consider whether expectation of success was reasonable and solutions were predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP rationales for concluding obviousness (F) Known work prompting predictable variations
rubrics_metrics.description: "Known work in one field of endeavor may prompt variations of it for use in either the same field or a different one based on design incentives or other market forces if the variations are predictable to PHOSITA."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess cross-field promptings and whether the variations would have been predictable to a person of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP rationales for concluding obviousness (G) Teaching, Suggestion, or Motivation (TSM)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation [TSM test] in the prior art that would have led PHOSITA to modify the prior art reference or to combine prior art reference teachings to arrive at the claimed invention" is a recognized rationale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-KSR, TSM need not be a rigid, explicit rule; motivation may be found implicitly in prior art, common sense, or market forces. Do not apply TSM as a mechanistic, mandatory formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims interpretation — broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with specification
rubrics_metrics.description: During prosecution claims are to be given their reasonable broadest interpretation consistent with PHOSITA’s interpretation of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret claim language as PHOSITA would reasonably read it in light of the specification when assessing obviousness and other patentability issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person Having Ordinary Skill in the Art (PHOSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: PHOSITA is a hypothetical person presumed to have known all the relevant art at the time of the invention; not definable solely by credentials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors for determining level of skill include: (A) type of problems encountered in the art; (B) prior art solutions to those problems; (C) rapidity with which innovations are made; (D) sophistication of the technology; (E) educational level of active workers in the field. One factor may dominate. Examiners may rely on their technical expertise to describe PHOSITA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding hindsight/ex-post facto analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: An Examiner should be aware of and avoid distortion caused by hindsight bias—reading into the prior art the teachings of the invention; must cast the mind back to the time the invention was made and occupy the mind of PHOSITA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hindsight is inferred when the understanding leading to the modification of prior art is not explained. Empirical studies show providing the solution increases hindsight bias. Passive jury instructions have little mitigating effect; examiners should actively explain reasoning and forget knowledge of the invention when assessing prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factors — scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the scope and content of the prior art as the first Graham inquiry for assessing obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurately identify prior art references and their disclosures. This is a necessary first step in obviousness analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factors — ascertain differences between prior art and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascertain differences between the prior art and the claims as part of the Graham analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly list claim limitations not found in prior art and evaluate whether those differences would have been obvious to PHOSITA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factors — resolve the level of PHOSITA
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve the level of ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA) as a Graham factor to maintain objectivity in the obviousness inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the PHOSITA factors (type of problems, prior art solutions, rapidity, sophistication, education) to set the reference point for what is obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factors — secondary considerations (objective indicia)
rubrics_metrics.description: When in doubt, inquire into secondary considerations such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, licensing, professional approval, copying, and praise from infringers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary evidence may rebut a prima facie case of obviousness but must be assessed objectively: establish nexus between invention and commercial success or between licensing and invention (e.g., license not just to avoid infringement). A presumption of nexus exists when the commercially successful device is the claimed invention, but the inventor must still show the success is due to the claimed features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination inventions — new synergy requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent merely arranges old elements with each performing their known function and yields no more than expected from such arrangement, the combination is obvious; to overcome obviousness the combined elements must create some new synergy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for evidence of unexpected properties or new synergistic effect beyond predictable aggregation. If prior art teaches away from combining elements, discovery of a successful means of combining them is more likely to be non-obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulated reasoning requirement (BPAI standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections on obviousness grounds cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be some articulated reasoning with a rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should provide specific, reasoned explanations showing why PHOSITA would have been motivated to combine references and why the combination would be predictable. Vague assertions are insufficient (per BPAI decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellant burden on appeal to BPAI
rubrics_metrics.description: On appeal to the Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences (BPAI), the appellant has the burden to demonstrate error in the Examiner’s position by showing insufficient evidence of prima facie obviousness or by rebutting the prima facie case with evidence of secondary indicia of non-obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellants should either attack the Examiner’s prima facie case (e.g., show lack of motivation/readings) or present objective indicia (nexus, commercial success, long-felt need) to rebut obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural routes and remedies (prosecution and review)
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor may request continued examination within six months after denial, appeal to the BPAI, request rehearing, request re-examination during enforceability, file civil action under 35 U.S.C. §145, or appeal to the Federal Circuit and petition for certiorari to the Supreme Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand timelines (e.g., six months for RCE), available forums (BPAI, Federal Circuit), and standards of review when strategizing responses to rejections and appeals.
